content: This updated Cochrane Review, which includes two additional studies since its last publication in 2019, evaluates the use of pregabalin as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition affecting approximately 1% of the UK population, with about one-third of these individuals continuing to experience seizures despite treatment with antiepileptic drugs. Pregabalin, a newer antiepileptic medication, has been developed to improve outcomes in such cases. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of pregabalin as an adjunctive treatment for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing pregabalin to placebo or other antiepileptic drugs in individuals of any age with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Both double-blind and single-blind trials were eligible for inclusion. The primary outcome was achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, while secondary outcomes included seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal for any reason, withdrawal due to adverse effects, and the proportion of participants experiencing adverse effects. The review included 11 RCTs involving 3949 participants. Nine trials compared pregabalin to placebo. Participants receiving pregabalin were significantly more likely to achieve a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 1.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.40 to 2.72, based on 9 trials with 2663 participants; low-certainty evidence). A dose-response relationship was observed, with the odds of achieving this outcome doubling when the dose increased from 300 mg/day to 600 mg/day (odds ratio [OR] 1.99, 95% CI 1.74 to 2.28). Pregabalin was also significantly associated with seizure freedom (RR 3.94, 95% CI 1.50 to 10.37, based on 4 trials with 1125 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, participants receiving pregabalin were more likely to discontinue treatment for any reason (RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.60; moderate-certainty evidence) and specifically due to adverse effects (RR 2.60, 95% CI 1.86 to 3.64; moderate-certainty evidence). Common adverse effects associated with pregabalin included ataxia, dizziness, somnolence, weight gain, headache, and fatigue. Three trials compared pregabalin to active control drugs (lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and gabapentin). Pregabalin was significantly more effective than lamotrigine in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.12; 1 trial with 293 participants). However, no significant differences were observed when pregabalin was compared to levetiracetam (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.11; 1 trial with 509 participants) or gabapentin (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.12; 1 trial with 484 participants). Regarding seizure freedom, no significant differences were found between pregabalin and lamotrigine (RR 1.39, 95% CI 0.40 to 4.83). However, fewer participants achieved seizure freedom with pregabalin compared to levetiracetam (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.85). Data on seizure freedom were not reported for the comparison between pregabalin and gabapentin. No significant differences were detected in treatment withdrawal rates for any reason or due to adverse effects when comparing pregabalin to active control drugs. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was rated as low or unclear, although there was a high risk of funding bias since all studies were sponsored by Pfizer. The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low to moderate using the GRADE approach. In conclusion, pregabalin, when used as an add-on treatment for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, was significantly more effective than placebo in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency and seizure freedom. Efficacy was observed at doses ranging from 150 mg/day to 600 mg/day, with greater effectiveness at higher doses, although tolerability issues were noted at 600 mg/day. The trials included in this review were of short duration, and longer-term studies are needed to guide clinical decision-making. These findings are specific to drug-resistant focal epilepsy and cannot be generalized to generalized epilepsies or to the use of pregabalin as monotherapy.
